title: How to Prioritize 401(k), Roth IRA, and HSA Contributions for Retirement
description: The 'Golden Order' of saving to maximize tax efficiency.
content:
When you have extra money to save, you face a menu of acronyms: 401(k), 403(b), IRA, HSA. Each has different tax rules and limits. Choosing the wrong order can cost you thousands in taxes or missed free money. The optimal strategy is a 'Waterfall': fill the most valuable bucket first, then let the money spill over into the next. This guide outlines the mathematically superior order of operations for funding your retirement accounts.

Key Takeaways

  • Step 1: The Match. Always contribute enough to your 401(k) to get the full employer match. This is a 100% ROI. Nothing beats free money.
  • Step 2: The HSA. If eligible, the Health Savings Account is the best account in the tax code (Triple Tax Advantage). Max this before IRAs.
  • Step 3: The Roth IRA. Tax-free growth and flexible withdrawals make this the next priority. Maximize the $7,000 limit.
  • Step 4: The Rest of 401(k). Go back to the 401(k) to fill the remaining space ($23,500) to lower your current year tax bill.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 2025 limits are: 401(k) $23,500; IRA $7,000; HSA $4,300 (Single). High earners can also use the 'Mega Backdoor Roth' to contribute up to $69,000 total if their plan allows. Knowing your limits prevents penalties.

The Waterfall Logic

Why this order matters.

1. The Match (Free Money)

If you put in $1 and boss puts in $1, you doubled your money instantly. Risk-free.
Action: Set payroll deduction to the match % (e.g., 5%).

2. The HSA (Triple Tax)

Better than Roth because contributions are tax-deductible (Pre-Tax) AND withdrawals are tax-free (for health).
Action: Max it out. Invest it. Don't spend it.

3. Roth IRA (Tax Control)

You control the investments (low fees) and tax treatment.
Action: Auto-transfer $583/mo to Fidelity/Vanguard.

4. Traditional 401(k) (Tax Drag)

The remaining balance reduces your taxable income today.
Action: Increase payroll deduction until you hit the $23,500 cap.

5. Taxable Brokerage (Liquidity)

Only after steps 1-4 are full.

Caveats and Adjustments

  1. High Income Earners: If you are in the 32%+ tax bracket, you might swap Step 3 and Step 4. The immediate tax deduction of the Traditional 401(k) might be worth more than the Roth benefit.
  2. Bad 401(k) Plan: If your employer plan has high fees (1%+ expense ratios), definitely stick to the Match only, then fill IRA/HSA/Taxable. Don't trap money in a bad plan.
  3. Early Retirement (FIRE): You might prioritize Taxable Brokerage (Step 5) earlier to build a 'Bridge' fund accessible before age 59.5.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I do both 401k and IRA?

Yes. The limits are separate. You can put $23,500 in 401k AND $7,000 in IRA. Total $30,500.

What if I don't have an HSA?

Skip Step 2. Go straight to Roth IRA. HSAs require a High Deductible Health Plan (HDHP).

Does the match count toward the limit?

No. The $23,500 limit is for your contributions. The employer match is on top of that (up to the $69,000 total limit).
